target_refs.quote: 9. The abandonment of the premises by M.L. Aggarwal, one of the erstwhile partners of the initial tenant (firm), he also being a Director in the company which had been accepted as tenant w.e.f. 27.03.1990 and the retention of the premises by R.P. Aggarwal, the other Director in the company were events which had no approval or consent of the landlord.

element_targets.reason: The target court anchored the operative change in possession/control to events after the company became tenant in 1990 and after the directors parted ways in April 1992, necessarily placing the relevant transfer well after 9 June 1952. The frozen input contains those admitted dates and the later use-and-occupation facts, so it is sufficient for this target.

target_refs.quote: This constitutes unauthorized assigning or subletting within the mischief of the provision contained in Section 14 (1)(b) of Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.

element_targets.reason: The target court used the undifferentiated conclusion 'assigning or subletting' but did not separately find a landlord-and-tenant relationship between the first and second respondents or the specific incidents of tenancy required by the GIVEN subletting route. A definite C02 status therefore cannot be extracted without choosing one side of the court's disjunctive reasoning.

target_refs.quote: This constitutes unauthorized assigning or subletting within the mischief of the provision contained in Section 14 (1)(b) of Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.

element_targets.reason: Although the target court expressly referred to 'assigning or subletting,' it did not separately decide that the tenant divested itself of all rights held as tenant, as C03 requires. The route-specific result is therefore ambiguous rather than a definite satisfied or defeated assignment finding.

target_refs.quote: It is the second respondent, in which R.P.Aggarwal is a Director, which has instead taken over the exclusive control of the subject premises.

element_targets.reason: The target court affirmatively found that the second respondent had taken over exclusive control of the premises, which substantively resolves the possession-divestment condition in favor of C04. The frozen input contains the admitted corporate split, R.P. Aggarwal's continued presence, and the second respondent's conceded use and occupation, so no decisive unavailable evidence is necessary to support this target.

target_refs.quote: It is a stranger in the premises whose presence is indisputably without the prior consent in writing of the petitioner landlord.

element_targets.reason: The target court expressly found the second respondent's presence to be indisputably without prior written consent. The frozen input, however, contains only the landlord's allegation of no written consent and omits the lease clause text and any independent admission or proof that made the target court treat the absence of written consent as indisputable; therefore input_sufficient is false.

target_refs.quote: It is the second respondent, in which R.P.Aggarwal is a Director, which has instead taken over the exclusive control of the subject premises.

element_targets.reason: The qualification depends on the tenant retaining legal possession while another person merely uses the premises. The target court instead accepted that the second respondent had taken over exclusive control, so the retained-possession/concurrent-use qualification did not apply. The frozen input contains the corporate-control and use-and-occupation facts needed to distinguish this from mere concurrent use.

cases.procedural_outcome_separate: The Delhi High Court set aside the ARC and Rent Control Tribunal orders rejecting the Section 14(1)(b) ground, allowed the eviction petition on that ground, and passed an eviction order in respect of the subject premises.
coverage_limits: The target court's phrase 'unauthorized assigning or subletting' does not distinguish the C02 subletting route from the C03 assignment route; those route-specific targets are therefore left without a definite status and marked as ambiguous reasoning.

For C05, the frozen input does not contain the lease clause (vi) text or independent proof/admission establishing the absence of written consent, even though the target court treated that absence as indisputable.

element_targets.reason: The judgment recited the statutory post-9-June-1952 requirement and the petitioner's allegation that the asserted transfer occurred after June 1952, but because it rejected the existence of subletting/parting on other grounds it did not separately adjudicate the timing condition.

target_refs.quote: In these circumstances, therefore, I am of the considered opinion that in the light of the above mentioned reasonings and relying upon above mentioned judgment, the petitioner has not been able to show that respondent no. 1 has subletted the tenanted premises to respondent no. 2.

element_targets.reason: The target court held that the petitioner failed to prove subletting to respondent no. 2, so the subletting route was not established. This is a burden failure, not a factual finding that a tenant-subtenant relationship was affirmatively false. The target reasoning relied in part on documents said to show that S.R. Printers remained in respondent no. 1's name and proprietorship; those documents are not included in the frozen input, whose evidence array is empty, so input_sufficient is false.

Although the petition used the word 'assigned,' the target court framed and decided the case around alleged subletting and retention of legal possession. It did not separately adjudicate whether respondent no. 1 had divested himself of all tenant rights under an assignment route.

target_refs.quote: 1 is having the full control over the said tenanted shop for which the petitioner has not been able to show anything to the contrary except his oral evidence which has been countered by the respondents in their respective oral evidence.
Therefore, petitioner has been failed to show from the record that there is subletting in this case, therefore, he is not entitled to an order of eviction u/s. 14 (1) (b) of DRC Act.

element_targets.reason: The court treated the petitioner's proof as insufficient to establish that respondent no. 1 had divested himself of possession or the right to possession; it emphasized the unrebutted assertion of continuing control. The truth of divestment therefore remains unknown rather than false. The court also relied on unspecified documents showing the continuing S.R. Printers proprietorship, which are absent from the frozen input, so input_sufficient is false.

The petitioner alleged lack of written consent, but the target court dismissed the Section 14(1)(b) ground because subletting/parting was not proved and did not separately decide whether written consent was absent.

target_refs.quote: In the above cited judgment of "Shyam Sunder Daniya v/s. J.D. Prabhu, 2007 (1) RCR (rent) 328 (HC)", it has been held that if the legal possession is retained by the original tenant then, it is not a case of subletting.
14. Similar is the situation present here in this case.

1 is having the full control over the said tenanted shop for which the petitioner has not been able to show anything to the contrary except his oral evidence which has been countered by the respondents in their respective oral evidence.

element_targets.reason: The target court expressly adopted the retained-legal-possession qualification and then said the present case was similar: the son was managing the business, while the petitioner failed to displace respondent no. 1's asserted continuing control. The legal qualification was therefore applied, but the underlying factual truth of retained control is not converted from burden failure into TRUE. Because the court also relied on omitted documentary material about the continuing proprietorship, input_sufficient is false.

cases.procedural_outcome_separate: The CCJ/ARC dismissed the eviction petition under Section 14(1)(b) without costs.
coverage_limits: The target court did not separately adjudicate the post-9-June-1952 timing condition, the assignment route, or the absence-of-written-consent condition after finding that subletting/parting had not been proved.

For C02, C04, and C06, the target reasoning relied in part on unspecified documents showing that the printing business remained in the name/proprietorship of respondent no. 1; those documents are absent from the frozen input, so those targets are marked input_sufficient=false.
The court's failure-of-proof reasoning does not justify labeling the disputed possession facts FALSE; fact_truth remains UNKNOWN where the basis is burden not carried.
